lesson_title: One Road or Many: Ohm's Law and Resistor Networks
hook_text: Add a resistor and the resistance goes DOWN? Yes — if you add it sideways. Here's the trick your bill depends on.
clip_script: Quick riddle: you add a resistor to a circuit and the total resistance goes DOWN. How? Think traffic. Resistors in a row are roadblocks on one road — every car queues through all of them, so more roadblocks, slower road. Just add them up: 4 plus 12 is 16 ohms. But wire a resistor in PARALLEL and you haven't added a roadblock — you've opened a whole new road between the same two taxi ranks. More roads, more traffic flowing, LESS total opposition. That same 4 and 12 side by side? Three ohms. Smaller than either one. Product over sum: 48 over 16. Your house is built on this trick — every appliance on its own road, all getting the full 230 volts, each switching off without killing the rest. Then the exam circuit: one resistor, then a parallel pair. Four moves, always: SHRINK the network to one number. Find the TOTAL current. SPEND the volts along the loop. SPLIT the amps between the branches — smaller resistor grabs the bigger share. And check yourself like an accountant: the branch currents must add back to what arrived. If the books balance, the marks are yours.
visual_style: Animated taxis queuing through roadblocks on a single road, then splitting joyfully across three parallel roads; circuit diagrams morphing into road maps and back; a four-step checklist stamping down over a solved network.
mood: Street-smart and confident — the circuit as a city you already know how to drive.
pacing: Riddle hook, rolling traffic middle, rapid four-beat method finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and walk any circuit in four moves.
